name: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with Big Buck Pads
title: Climb Right Spurs: Aluminum Climbers with Big Buck Pads
h1: Climb Right Spurs: Aluminum Climbers with Big Buck Pads
meta: Climb Right spurs with aluminum shanks and Big Buck pads: light aluminum spikes for removal climbers who spend all day on the stem. Typical price and fit tips.
tagline: Light aluminum removal spurs with wide, padded uppers for long days on spikes.
summary: Climb Right spurs pair lightweight aluminum shanks with Big Buck style pads, so you carry less weight on every step and spread the load across your calf. They suit removal climbers who are on spikes for hours, not minutes.
highlights: Aluminum shanks cut weight compared with steel climbers
Big Buck pads spread pressure across the upper calf
Replaceable tree gaffs for sharpening and swap-outs
Adjustable shank length to fit your leg
Built for removals, not for pruning live trees

p: Every pound on your ankle gets lifted with every step. On a big removal you might take a few hundred steps up and down the stem, and that is where aluminum spikes earn their price. The shanks are noticeably lighter than a steel pair, so your legs feel fresher by the time you are tying in for the last few picks.

Aluminum is not the right choice for every crew. Steel shanks take more abuse from rocks, truck beds and being thrown on the ground, and they cost less. If you climb on spurs a few times a month, a steel pair is often the better value. If you are a removal specialist working spikes all week, the lighter set pays you back in reduced fatigue.

Pads are where most spur discomfort starts. Thin pads and narrow straps press into the top of your calf and the shin, and after an hour that pressure is all you can think about. The Big Buck pad is a wide, stiff, padded upper that wraps more of the leg, so load is spread over a larger area and the shank is held steadier against your boot.

A steadier shank also helps the gaff bite cleanly. When the upper flops around, the gaff can roll out of the bark on a hard kick. Wide pads keep the climber aligned with your leg so you can trust each step. If you already own pads you like, compare this set with the other aluminum spurs before you buy.

body.h: Setting them up and caring for them
p: Set shank length so the top of the shank sits a couple of fingers below the bend of your knee. Too long and it digs in when you bend; too short and you lose leverage. Wear a stiff boot with a steel shank in the sole, since a soft boot lets the stirrup fold your arch over time.

Keep gaffs sharp with a file, following the original bevel, and replace them when they get short or chipped. Check strap stitching, buckles and pads before each climb. Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes.

body.h: Where they fit in your kit
p: Spurs are for removals and emergency rescue, not for pruning or climbing a tree you plan to keep. Each gaff hole is a wound. Pair your spurs with a flip line or steel-core lanyard, a good saddle and a second attachment point when you are cutting. A well-fitted pair of Climb Right spurs with Big Buck pads is a solid base for that removal setup.

Before you order, measure from the floor to just below the bend of your knee while wearing your climbing boots. That number tells you whether the shank adjustment range fits you, and it saves a return.

faq.q: Are aluminum spikes as strong as steel?
faq.a: Aluminum shanks are designed for the loads of climbing, but they are softer than steel and dent more easily if abused. Store them carefully and inspect them for cracks or bends before each use.

faq.q: Can I put Big Buck pads on other spurs?
faq.a: Big Buck pads are designed around specific climber shanks. Check the manufacturer's fit information before mixing brands.

faq.q: Can I use spurs for pruning?
faq.a: No. Spurs wound the tree, so use them only for removals or rescue. Prune live trees with a rope and saddle system.

name: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with Steel Support Pads
title: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with Steel Support Pads
h1: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with Steel Support Pads
meta: Climb Right aluminum climbers with steel support pads: light shanks plus rigid uppers that keep the spur aligned on removals. Typical price and fit tips.
tagline: Lightweight aluminum climbers with stiff steel-backed pads for removal climbers.
summary: Climb Right aluminum climbers with steel support pads keep weight down while a rigid support in the upper pad holds the shank steady against your leg. They are a good match for climbers who want a firm, locked-in feel on removals.
highlights: Aluminum shanks for less weight per step
Steel support in the pad keeps the spur aligned

p: These climbers combine aluminum shanks with pads that carry a steel support. The stiff upper resists twisting, which keeps the gaff angle consistent when you kick in on rough bark or work around a stem. Climbers who dislike the softer feel of all-foam pads tend to like this setup.

Because the shanks are aluminum, you save weight on every step compared with steel climbers. Over a full day of removals that adds up. Compare this set with the Big Buck pad version in our aluminum spurs section if you want a wider, softer pad.

Set the shank so it sits just below the bend of the knee and wear a stiff boot with a steel shank. Keep gaffs sharp along the factory bevel and replace them when worn. Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes. Use spurs only for removals, never for pruning a tree that will stay.

Before you order, measure from the floor to just below the bend of your knee in your climbing boots, and check that it falls inside the shank adjustment range. Pair the climbers with a flip line or steel-core lanyard and keep a second attachment point when you cut.

faq.q: Who are steel support pads for?
faq.a: Climbers who want a rigid, locked-in upper that keeps the spur from rolling. Some people find wider soft pads more comfortable, so try both if you can.

faq.q: Do these climbers come with tree gaffs?
faq.a: They are set up for tree work with replaceable gaffs. Confirm the gaff type with the seller before ordering.

name: Buckingham Steel Climbers with Big Buck Pads
title: Buckingham Climbing Spikes with Big Buck Pads (Steel)
h1: Buckingham Climbing Spikes: Steel Climbers with Big Buck Pads
meta: Buckingham climbing spikes with steel shanks and Big Buck pads: tough, adjustable tree spikes for removal work. Typical price, fit advice and gaff care tips.
tagline: Tough steel Buckingham spikes with wide Big Buck pads for everyday removal work.
summary: These Buckingham climbing spikes pair durable steel shanks with Big Buck pads, a combination many removal climbers run as their everyday set. Steel takes a beating on the truck and the job, while the wide pads keep your calves comfortable on long climbs.
highlights: Steel shanks that stand up to hard use
Big Buck pads spread load across the calf
Lower straps hold the boot securely

body.h: Steel Buckingham spikes for daily removals
p: Buckingham spikes have been a standard on tree crews for a long time, and the steel version is the workhorse. It weighs more than aluminum, but steel shrugs off getting tossed in a gear bin, dragged over rocks or stepped on in the yard. For a crew set that gets passed around, that toughness matters more than a few ounces.
The shanks adjust for leg length, and the gaffs are replaceable, so a good pair of Buckingham tree climbing spikes can last years with new straps, pads and gaffs along the way.

Buckingham spikes are also easy to service. Because the parts are widely stocked, a crew can keep several sets running for years by swapping straps and gaffs as they wear rather than retiring the whole climber.

Big Buck pads are wide, padded uppers that wrap the calf. The width spreads load and stops the buck spur from rocking, which keeps the gaff angle consistent on each kick. Climbers moving from basic strap uppers usually notice the difference in the first hour.
If your current pads are worn out, you can buy replacement climber pads on their own instead of a whole new set of climbers.

Big Buck pads also help on stems with rough or thick bark, where you need a firm kick to set the gaff. A pad that holds the shank tight against the leg puts that force straight into the point instead of letting the climber twist.

The lower straps wrap the boot and hold the stirrup in place. Run them snug, not crushing, with the stirrup under the arch of a stiff boot with a steel shank. A soft boot lets the stirrup fold your foot and leads to sore arches. A buck strap for tree climbing only works if the boot under it is stiff.
Check strap leather or webbing for cuts and cracking. Replace straps before they look marginal, not after.

Pay attention to how the straps wear at the buckle. That is where leather cracks and webbing frays first. A climber that slips on the boot mid-climb is a serious problem, so treat straps as a wear item and keep a spare set in the truck.

Sharpen gaffs with a file along the factory bevel; never grind them on a wheel, which can overheat the steel. Replace gaffs when they get short. Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes.
Use spurs for removals only. Every gaff hole wounds the tree, so prune live trees from a rope system instead.

Store spurs with gaff guards on. Guards protect the points and protect you, your rope and your truck seats from a sharp gaff. Keep spurs out of the bottom of the gear bin where other tools can bend the gaffs or crush the pads.

faq.q: Are steel or aluminum Buckingham spikes better?
faq.a: Steel is tougher and less expensive; aluminum is lighter. Daily removal climbers often go light, while crews sharing gear usually choose steel.

faq.q: Can I replace just the pads or gaffs?
faq.a: Yes. Pads, straps and gaffs are all replaceable parts, so you can rebuild a set instead of buying new climbers.

faq.q: What boots should I wear with climbing spikes?
faq.a: A stiff, high-ankle work boot with a steel shank in the sole supports your arch on the stirrup. Many climbers use dedicated lineman or climbing boots.

highlights: Add your choice of upper pads

p: Not everyone wants the same upper. Some climbers swear by wide Big Buck pads, others prefer T-pads or steel support uppers. This set gives you steel Buckingham climbers with lower straps so you can add the pads that fit your leg and your work.
Steel shanks handle rough treatment in the truck and on the job. Browse climber pads to finish the set.

Buying the climbers on their own also makes sense if you already have good pads from a retired set. Swap them across, fit new lower straps if needed, and you have a working pair of Buckingham climbing spikes for less than a complete new set.

You need upper pads and straps fitted before these climbers go on your legs. Set shank length just below the bend of the knee and wear stiff boots with a steel shank. Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes. Use spurs for removals only, not for pruning.
Keep gaffs sharp along the factory bevel and replace them when they get short or damaged.
Store them with gaff guards on so the points stay sharp and do not damage rope or other gear in the truck.

faq.q: Do these come with upper pads?
faq.a: This listing is for the climbers with lower straps. Plan on adding upper pads and straps before use.

faq.q: Which pads should I add?
faq.a: Big Buck pads are a popular wide, comfortable choice. T-pads are a lighter, more traditional option.

name: Buckingham Steel Climbers with T-Pads
title: Buckingham Tree Spikes with T-Pads (Steel Climbers)
h1: Buckingham Tree Spikes: Steel Climbers with T-Pads
meta: Buckingham tree spikes with steel shanks and classic T-pads: a lighter, simpler upper on tough steel climbers. Typical price, fit advice and gaff care tips.
tagline: Steel Buckingham tree spikes with traditional T-pad uppers for removal climbers.
summary: These Buckingham tree spikes combine steel shanks with T-pads, a traditional upper that is lighter and less bulky than wide wrap pads. Many climbers like the T-pad for its simple, close fit and easy strap adjustment.
highlights: Steel shanks for long service life
T-pad uppers with a close, low-bulk fit
Pairs well with stiff steel-shank climbing boots

p: The T-pad is the traditional upper on Buckingham spikes. It is a T-shaped pad that sits against the calf with a strap around the leg. It carries less bulk than a full wrap pad, so it packs smaller and feels less hot in summer.

Paired with steel shanks, these Buckingham climbing spikes are a durable, straightforward removal set. If you want more comfort for long days, look at the Big Buck pad version in our Buckingham steel spurs lineup.

Steel shanks are the practical choice for crews that share gear or climbers who only spike a few removals a month. They cost less than aluminum and handle rough storage, so Buckingham tree spikes like these can live in the truck and still be ready when the next removal comes in.

Spurs only work as well as the boot under them. Look for tree climbing boots with a steel shank in the sole and good ankle support. The stirrup sits under the arch, and a stiff sole keeps it from bending your foot on every step.

Snug the lower strap around the boot so the stirrup cannot slide, and set the upper strap firm but not tight enough to cut off circulation. Adjust shank length so the top sits just below the bend in your knee.

If your feet hurt after a day on spurs, look at the boot before the spur. Tree climbing boots with a steel shank spread the stirrup load across the sole, and a boot with a defined heel keeps the stirrup from sliding forward.

Sharpen gaffs with a file along the factory bevel and keep the point sharp enough to bite without a hard kick. Replace gaffs that are short, chipped or bent. Check pads and straps for wear, cuts and cracked leather.

Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes. Spurs belong on removals and rescues only; climb live trees on rope.
Keep gaff guards on whenever the spurs are off your legs, both to protect the points and to keep a sharp gaff away from your rope and the truck seats.

On a removal, set your flip line around the stem before you start climbing and keep it adjusted so you can lean back into it. Climb with short, deliberate steps and set each gaff at a slight angle into the wood rather than flat against the bark.

When you reach your work position, set a second attachment before you start the saw. Spurs give you footing, but your lanyard and climbing line hold you. Rest often on long climbs; tired legs lead to sloppy kicks and cut-outs.

faq.q: Are T-pads comfortable?
faq.a: They are comfortable for many climbers, especially on shorter climbs. For all-day removals, wider pads like Big Buck pads spread load better.

faq.q: Do I need special boots for tree spikes?
faq.a: Use a stiff work or climbing boot with a steel shank in the sole. Soft hikers or sneakers are not suitable.

faq.q: Can I upgrade the pads later?
faq.a: Yes. Uppers are replaceable, so you can move to Big Buck pads without replacing the climbers.

name: Buckingham Big Buck Pads
title: Buckingham Big Buck Pads for Climbing Spurs
meta: Buckingham Big Buck pads are wide, padded uppers for buck spur climbers. Spread load across the calf and steady the shank on long removals. Typical price here.
tagline: Wide, padded replacement uppers that make long days on spurs easier on your calves.
summary: Buckingham Big Buck pads are wide replacement uppers for climbing spurs that spread pressure across the calf and keep the shank steady. They are a common upgrade for climbers whose stock pads dig in after an hour on the stem.
highlights: Holds the spur steady against the leg

p: Pads take the load when you stand in your spurs. Narrow or worn pads concentrate that load and leave bruises on the calf. Big Buck pads use a wider padded shell that wraps more of the leg, and the stiffer shape helps the buck spur stay aligned so the gaff bites cleanly.
They are a common upgrade for Buckingham steel spurs and other compatible climbers.

New pads are also cheaper than new climbers. If your shanks and gaffs are in good shape, replacing the uppers is often all it takes to make an old pair feel new. The buckle closure is easy to adjust with gloves and holds firm through a full day of kicking in on removals.

Confirm the pads fit your climber model before ordering. Mount them so the top of the pad sits below the bend in the knee and the straps close snug without pinching. Inspect stitching, buckles and padding before each climb, and replace pads that are cracked or torn. Spurs are life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be trained before climbing.
Keep a pair of gaff guards on your spurs during storage so the points do not cut into the new pads or straps.

faq.q: Will Big Buck pads fit my spurs?
faq.a: They are made for Buckingham climbers and some compatible models. Check the fit information before you buy.

faq.q: Buckle or hook-and-loop?
faq.a: This is the buckle version. A hook-and-loop closure version is also available for faster on and off.

name: Buckingham Big Buck Velcro Pads
title: Buckingham Big Buck Pads with Hook-and-Loop Closure
h1: Buckingham Big Buck Pads, Velcro Closure
meta: Buckingham Big Buck pads with a hook-and-loop closure: wide, padded spur uppers that go on and off fast between climbs. Fit notes and typical price inside.
tagline: Wide Big Buck uppers with a quick hook-and-loop closure for fast on and off.
summary: These Buckingham Big Buck pads use a hook-and-loop closure instead of buckles, so you can strap in and out of your spurs quickly. You still get the wide, padded upper that spreads load across the calf.
highlights: Spreads load and steadies the shank

p: On jobs where you go up and down several trees, buckles slow you down. The hook-and-loop closure on these Big Buck pads lets you snug the upper in one move and pull it off just as fast. The wide padded shell still wraps the calf to reduce pressure points and keep the spur aligned.
Shop other climber pads if you prefer a buckle closure.

That speed is useful on lot clearing and storm work, where you might top and drop several trees in a morning. It also makes it easier to loosen the upper during a break on the ground, which helps circulation on long days on spikes.

Hook-and-loop loses grip when packed with sawdust, bark and pitch. Brush it clean regularly and replace pads when the closure no longer holds firmly. Check fit with your climber model before ordering. Inspect pads and straps before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be trained before climbing on spurs.

If you climb in wet, muddy or icy conditions often, consider the buckle version, which is less affected by debris. Many climbers keep one of each and choose by the job. Store spurs with gaff guards on so points cannot catch the closure.

faq.q: Is hook-and-loop as secure as buckles?
faq.a: When clean and in good condition it holds well. Debris weakens it, so keep it clean and replace pads when grip fades.

faq.q: Do these fit all spurs?
faq.a: They are designed for Buckingham climbers and some compatible models. Confirm fit before ordering.

name: Lightweight Tree Climbing Spurs
title: Lightweight Tree Spikes: Climbing Spurs for Removals
h1: Lightweight Tree Spikes and Climbing Spurs
meta: Lightweight tree spikes for removal climbers: what to look for in aluminum climbing spurs, pads, gaffs and boots, plus fit and safety tips. Typical price here.
tagline: Light climbing spurs for removal climbers who want less weight on every step.
summary: Lightweight tree spikes cut the weight you lift with every step, which makes a real difference on big removals. This guide covers what to look for in lightweight climbing spurs, from shank material to pads, gaffs and boots.

p: On a big removal you might spend most of the day on spurs. Every ounce on your ankle is lifted on each step, so lightweight tree climbing spurs reduce fatigue in your hips, knees and calves. Climbers who switch from heavy steel usually notice it the first afternoon.
The trade-off is cost and toughness. Light alloy shanks cost more and can dent or bend if dropped on rock or thrown in a truck bed. Treat them like the tool they are and they will last.
Lightweight climbing spikes also help on travel-heavy work like storm cleanup, where you may hike gear into a back lot or carry it up a slope. Less weight in the bag makes the whole day easier.

body.h: What to look for in climbing spurs
p: Start with pads. A wide, well-padded upper spreads load and keeps the shank aligned. Next look at gaffs: replaceable tree gaffs let you swap worn points without buying new climbers. Then check adjustment range so the top of the shank sits just below the bend of your knee.
Straps should be easy to adjust with gloves on and easy to replace. Compare options in aluminum spurs and steel spurs before deciding.

Look at how the climbing spurs fasten as well. Buckles are secure and easy to adjust with gloves. Hook-and-loop closures are faster but lose grip when packed with sawdust. Pick the style that matches how often you get in and out of your spurs.

Tree climber spikes need a stiff boot with a steel shank in the sole. The stirrup sits under the arch, and a soft sole lets it fold your foot. High ankle support helps when you are standing sideways on a stem.
Snug the lower strap so the stirrup cannot shift, and set the upper strap firm without cutting off circulation.

Before buying, measure from the floor to just below the bend of your knee while wearing your boots. That tells you whether a spur's adjustment range fits your leg. Climbers with very long or short legs should check this carefully.

Spurs are for removals and emergency rescue only. Every gaff hole wounds the tree, so climb trees you are keeping on rope. Always work with a flip line or steel-core lanyard and keep two points of attachment when cutting.

Climbing spurs are part of your fall-protection system. Inspect gaffs, shanks, straps and pads before every climb, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and get trained before you climb on spikes.
Store spurs with gaff guards on, keep them away from other tools that can bend gaffs, and sharpen with a file only. Replace gaffs, straps and pads as they wear so the whole system stays dependable.

faq.q: How much lighter are aluminum spurs than steel?
faq.a: It varies by model and pads, but aluminum shanks are noticeably lighter than steel. Check the maker's listed weight for the exact set you are considering.

faq.q: Are lightweight spurs strong enough?
faq.a: Spurs from reputable makers are built for climbing loads. Light alloys dent more easily than steel, so inspect them before each climb and retire damaged parts.

faq.q: Can I use tree spikes for pruning?
faq.a: No. Use spurs only for removals or rescue. Prune live trees from a rope and saddle system.

name: Buckingham Buckalloy Screw and Dowel Style Replacement Tree Gaffs
title: Buckingham Replacement Gaffs: Buckalloy Screw and Dowel
h1: Buckingham Replacement Gaffs: Buckalloy Screw and Dowel Style
meta: Buckingham replacement gaffs in Buckalloy, screw and dowel style: fresh tree gaffs for worn spurs. When to replace gaffs and how to fit them. Typical price.
tagline: Screw and dowel style Buckalloy tree gaffs to bring worn Buckingham spurs back.
summary: These Buckingham replacement gaffs are Buckalloy tree gaffs in the screw and dowel mounting style. Swap them in when your old gaffs are short, chipped or bent and get a confident bite back without buying new climbers.

p: Gaffs wear every time you sharpen them. Once they get short, the point no longer reaches through thick bark, and that is when cut-outs happen. Replace gaffs that are shortened past the maker's limit, chipped, cracked or bent. Do not try to straighten a bent gaff.
Match the mount style to your climbers. These are screw and dowel style; check your shanks before ordering from replacement gaffs and parts.

A fresh set of Buckingham replacement gaffs is one of the cheapest ways to make old climbers feel safer. Sharp, full-length gaffs set with a lighter kick, so you climb with less effort and less strain on your knees and ankles.

Install gaffs following the manufacturer's instructions and tighten the screws firmly. Sharpen with a file along the factory bevel and never on a grinder, which can overheat the metal. Spurs are life-support equipment: inspect before every climb, follow ANSI Z133, and be trained before climbing on spikes.
Always replace gaffs as a pair so both legs bite the same way. Keep gaff guards on whenever the spurs are off your legs to protect the new points and everything around them.

faq.q: Will these fit my spurs?
faq.a: They fit climbers that use screw and dowel style gaffs. Confirm your shank type before buying.

faq.q: Can I sharpen gaffs on a bench grinder?
faq.a: No. Heat can ruin the temper. Use a file and follow the original bevel.

name: Edelrid Talon Upper Strap System
title: Upper Strap System for Edelrid Talons
h1: Upper Strap System for Edelrid Talons
meta: Replacement upper strap system for Edelrid Talon spurs. Refresh worn uppers on your Edelrid Talons and keep the climber snug and steady. Typical price and tips.
tagline: Replacement upper straps and pads for Edelrid Talon climbing spurs.

highlights: Keeps your spurs in service longer
specs: Worn Talon upper straps and padding

Find gaffs and other parts in replacement gaffs and parts.

Edelrid Talons are popular with removal climbers who want a modern, adjustable spur, and the upper is the part that takes the most wear. Sweat, sawdust, bark and pitch all break down padding and straps over a season of hard use. Rather than living with a sloppy fit, replace the upper and get back the support the spur had when it was new.

Install the system following Edelrid's instructions and check that every strap closes securely before climbing. Inspect uppers, lower straps, shanks and gaffs before every climb. Spurs are life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be trained before you climb on spikes.

Keep the old upper as a reference while installing the new one, so straps go back in the same orientation. Store your Talons with gaff guards on, and keep the new upper away from fuel, bar oil and solvents.

faq.q: Does this fit other spurs?
faq.a: It is made for Edelrid Talon spurs. Do not mix it with other brands unless the manufacturer says it is compatible.

faq.q: When should I replace the upper?
faq.a: Replace it when padding is packed flat, straps are cut or frayed, or closures no longer hold firmly.

name: Big Shot Throw Weight Launcher
title: Big Shot Throw Line Launcher for Arborists
meta: The Big Shot throw line launcher sends a throw weight into high crotches you cannot reach by hand. A slingshot-style launcher on a pole for tall tree access.
tagline: Pole-mounted slingshot that puts a throw weight into high unions fast.
summary: The Big Shot throw line launcher is a pole-mounted slingshot that sends a throw weight much higher than most climbers can throw by hand. It is a go-to tool for setting lines in tall conifers and big hardwoods.
highlights: Launches throw weights well above hand-throw height
Pole-mounted for a stable, aimed shot
Works with standard throw weights and throw line
Speeds up line setting on tall trees
specs: Setting climbing lines in tall trees

p: Hand throwing tops out well below the best tie-in points on a tall tree. The Big Shot, sometimes called a bean bag launcher, uses heavy elastic bands on a pole to launch a throw weight high and straight. You aim, draw, release, and the weight carries the throw line over the union you picked.
Pair it with a good throw line and weights from our throw line kits and keep line flaked in a cube or bag so it pays out cleanly.

A launcher also helps when the best union is surrounded by dense foliage that eats hand throws. A fast, straight shot carries the weight through small gaps, so you set the line you wanted instead of settling for a lower, weaker tie-in.

Treat the launcher like the powerful tool it is. Never aim at people, vehicles, houses or power lines, and keep everyone out of the area where the weight can land or bounce. Wear eye protection and a helmet, and inspect bands and pouch for wear before each use. Throw lines and weights are used to set climbing lines, not to hold a climber. Always inspect the climbing line and anchor you install, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the drop zone clear when throwing.

faq.q: What weight should I use with a launcher?
faq.a: Use the weights recommended by the launcher maker. Weights that are too light drift and weights that are too heavy shorten range.

faq.q: Is a launcher worth it over hand throwing?
faq.a: If you regularly set lines in tall trees, yes. It saves time and gets you to better tie-in points.

name: Starter Throw Line Kit
title: Starter Throw Line Kit for Arborists
meta: A starter throw line kit gives new climbers the throw line, throw weights and storage they need to set a climbing line. What's inside and how to use it.
tagline: Throw line, weights and storage in one kit for new climbers.
summary: This starter throw line kit bundles the basics for setting a climbing line: arborist throw line, throw weights and a way to store the line so it pays out clean. It is the easy way to get a working setup without piecing it together.
highlights: Throw line and weights matched to each other
Good first setup for new climbers
Easy to add a second weight later

body.h: What a throw line kit does
p: Setting your climbing line starts on the ground. You throw a small weight attached to thin, slick line over the union you want, then use that line to pull your climbing rope into place. A good throw line arborist setup saves you dozens of wasted throws a day.
This kit gives you matched line and weights plus storage, so the line flakes out without knots. When you need more reach, look at the Big Shot launcher.

Keeping the parts together matters on the job. When your line, weights and storage live in one bag, you can grab the kit, set a line and get climbing without hunting through the truck for a missing weight or a tangled hank.

Practice an underhand two-hand throw on easy limbs before you need it on a job. Flake the line before each throw and keep your feet off it. Keep people clear of the landing zone and wear a helmet. Throw lines and weights are used to set climbing lines, not to hold a climber. Always inspect the climbing line and anchor you install, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the drop zone clear when throwing.

faq.q: What size throw weight should a beginner use?
faq.a: A mid-weight bag is easiest to learn with. Lighter weights travel farther but are harder to pull back through tight crotches.

faq.q: Can I use throw line as a climbing line?
faq.a: No. Throw line is only for setting your climbing line. It is not rated to hold a person.

name: Throw Line Storage Bag
title: Throw Line Bag and Storage for Arborists
meta: A throw line bag keeps your line flaked, clean and ready to pay out without tangles. Compare collapsible cubes and arborist throw bags, plus storage tips.
tagline: Collapsible storage that keeps throw line flaked, clean and tangle-free.
summary: A throw line bag stores your line loose and flaked so it feeds out cleanly on every throw. It keeps sawdust and dirt off the line and gives you a place to clip your throw weight between attempts.
highlights: Keeps line flaked and ready to throw
Protects line from dirt and debris
Clip point for your throw weight

p: Throw line is thin and slick. Left in a pile on the ground it picks up twigs and grass and tangles the moment you throw. Feeding it into a throw line cube or bag keeps it loose and flaked, so it pays out cleanly and you spend your time setting lines instead of untangling them.
Most climbers keep one throw line and bag together as a set. See throw weights and line for line to match.

Arborist throw bags and cubes also make it easy to keep two lines ready at once, which helps when you are isolating a crotch or setting a second line for rigging. Feed each line into its own bag so they never cross.

Feed line into the bag loosely by hand; do not coil it. Open the bag fully before you throw and stand it upright where you will not step in it. Shake out debris after each job and let it dry if wet. Throw lines and weights are used to set climbing lines, not to hold a climber. Always inspect the climbing line and anchor you install, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the drop zone clear when throwing.

faq.q: Cube or bag?
faq.a: Cubes stand open on their own, which makes them fast. Soft bags pack smaller. Both work if you feed line in loosely.

faq.q: How much line fits in a bag?
faq.a: Most hold a standard hank of throw line with room to spare. Check the size before buying for longer lengths.

name: Samson Zing-It 1.75mm Throw Line
title: Samson Zing It 1.75mm Throw Line
meta: Samson Zing It throw line is slick, light 1.75mm Dyneema cord built for fast throws and easy pull-through. A favorite arborist throwline. See typical price.
tagline: Slick, thin Dyneema throw line that slides through crotches with little drag.
summary: Samson Zing It is a slick 1.75 mm Dyneema throw line that many arborists consider the standard. Its coated finish slides over bark with little friction, so throws go farther and the line pulls back without hanging up.
highlights: Slick coating reduces friction over bark
Bright colors for easy tracking in the canopy

body.h: Why Zing It line is so popular
p: Throw line has one job: get over the union you want and come back down without snagging. Zing It line does that well because it is thin, light and slick. The low weight means your throw weight is not dragging much line behind it, and the coated Dyneema slides over bark instead of grabbing it.

That slickness also helps when you need to isolate a crotch or pull the weight back through a tight spot. Climbers who switch from cheaper nylon throw line usually notice the difference in the first few throws.

It is also easy to see. Zing It comes in bright colors that stand out against bark and leaves, which helps when you are trying to spot where the line went over and whether it is resting on the union you aimed for.

Flake the line into a cube or bag, clip your weight on with a simple knot or a small snap, and throw underhand with a smooth arc. Once over, lower the weight, tie on your climbing line and pull it through. Zing It is strong enough to pull most climbing lines into place but is not a climbing or rigging line.
Keep a throw line bag with your line so it stays clean and tangle-free between throws.
When a throw goes over the wrong limb, the slick finish helps. You can often flip or shake the line off a lower limb and drop it into the right crotch without starting over.

Dirt and sap make any throw line sticky. Shake out debris and keep line out of mud. Cut out damaged sections and retie your weight when the end gets fuzzy. Replace the line when the coating wears through or the core shows.

Throw line is not life-support equipment, but it sets the line that is. Always inspect your climbing line and tie-in point, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep people clear of the throw zone.
Keep a spare hank in the truck. Throw line gets cut, stuck high in a tree or left behind more often than any other piece of climbing gear, and a spare saves the job.

Zing It is about as thin as most arborists go. Some climbers prefer a slightly thicker throw line for easier handling with gloves or less tangling. If you use a launcher, thin slick line is usually the best match because it adds the least drag.

Most climbers settle on one throw line and stick with it, because the way a line runs off the cube and through the hand becomes muscle memory. If that is your first slick line, give it a few days of throwing before judging it.

faq.q: How strong is Zing It throw line?
faq.a: It is strong enough to pull climbing lines into place, but it is not rated for climbing or rigging. Check Samson's published figures for exact strength.

faq.q: Is Zing It good for a throw line launcher?
faq.a: Yes. Its low weight and slick finish make it a common choice with launchers.

faq.q: Why is my throw line tangling?
faq.a: Usually it is coiled instead of flaked. Feed it loosely into a bag or cube and keep debris out.

name: Target Line Throw Line
title: Target Line Throw Line for Tree Climbers
meta: Target Line throw line is a slick, light arborist throwline built for clean throws and easy pull-through in the canopy. How to use it and typical price.
tagline: Slick, lightweight throw line for setting climbing lines with less snagging.
summary: Target Line is a lightweight, slick throw line designed to carry a throw weight high into the canopy and come back without hanging up. It is a straightforward choice for climbers setting lines every day.
highlights: Light, slick construction for long throws
Pulls back through crotches with little drag
Bright color for tracking in the canopy
Works with standard throw weights and launchers

body.h: What makes a good throw line
p: A throw line has to be light enough that your weight can carry it a long way, slick enough to slide over bark, and stiff enough not to tangle the moment it hits the ground. Target Line is built around that balance. It runs cleanly out of a cube and does not grab when you pull the weight back to isolate a crotch.
Target lines also come in bright colors, which helps when you are tracking a line through dense leaves or trying to tell your throw line from a rigging line.

Line that is too soft tends to grab bark and bunch up when you pull it back. Line that is too stiff springs into loops on the ground. A good throw line sits between the two, which is what most climbers look for when they choose one for daily use.

body.h: Using Target Line on the job
p: Flake the line into a bag or cube, tie your throw weight on with a secure knot, and throw underhand in a smooth arc. Once the weight is over the union, lower it, tie on your climbing line and pull it into place. If you need to go higher than you can throw, a launcher will send the same line much farther.
Browse other throw line options if you want to compare diameter and feel.
Practice matters as much as the line. Spend time throwing at easy targets so your arc and release become consistent. Most missed throws come from rushing, not from the gear.
Keep the line clean, dry and out of mud. Cut out damaged sections and retie your weight when the end wears. Replace the line once the coating is worn through.

Throw line is not rated for climbing or rigging. It only sets the line that holds you, so always inspect your climbing system and anchor, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep people out of the throw zone.

If your line gets stuck high in a tree, do not yank on it from directly below. Change your angle, try to flip it free, and if it will not come down, cut it as high as you can reach and retie a weight on the remaining line.

Thinner lines carry farther and add less drag, especially with a launcher. Slightly thicker lines are easier to grip with gloves and tend to tangle less. Slick coatings help retrieval and isolation, while softer lines can grab bark.

Think about where you work. In big conifers and tall hardwoods, a light slick line paired with a launcher is hard to beat. On smaller residential trees, a line that handles well by hand matters more. Many climbers carry two lines so they always have a backup when one gets stuck or cut. Keep each in its own bag so target lines never get mixed with rigging gear.

faq.q: What diameter is Target Line?
faq.a: Check the product label for exact diameter and length. Most arborist throw lines fall between about 1.75 and 2.2 mm.

faq.q: Can I use Target Line with a launcher?
faq.a: Yes, a light slick throw line like this works well with pole launchers.

faq.q: How long does throw line last?
faq.a: It depends on use and conditions. Replace it when the coating wears through, it gets fuzzy, or it starts snagging.

name: Teufelberger DynaGlide Throw Line
title: Teufelberger DynaGlide Throw Line
meta: Teufelberger DynaGlide throw line is a slick, high-performance arborist throwline that slides over bark and pulls back clean. Features, care and typical price.
tagline: A slick, durable throw line built for clean throws and smooth pull-back.
summary: Teufelberger DynaGlide is a slick, durable throw line built to slide over bark and through tight crotches with little drag. Climbers like DynaGlide for its smooth feel in the hand and its resistance to tangling.
highlights: Slick finish reduces drag over bark
Works by hand or with a launcher

p: DynaGlide is known for being slick. That matters most when you are not just throwing over a union but working the line through the canopy: flipping it off a lower branch, pulling the weight back to isolate a crotch, or retrieving a stuck weight. A slick line lets those moves happen without fighting friction.
The construction also handles well. It flakes into a cube without much memory and comes out without knotting, so you spend less time clearing tangles between throws.
That handling makes DynaGlide a common choice for climbers who set many lines a day, such as on large pruning contracts or utility clearance, where every saved minute adds up across the crew.

Flake the line, tie on your throw weight, and throw underhand with a smooth arc. When the weight goes over, lower it to the ground, attach your climbing line and pull it over. If you are setting a canopy anchor or a basal tie, make sure the union you chose is sound before you load it.
Store DynaGlide in a throw line bag so it stays clean between jobs.
When the line lands over the wrong limb, try flipping or shaking it off before pulling it back. A slick line responds well to those small corrections, and you avoid a full rethrow.

Even slick line slows down when it is dirty. Shake debris out of the bag, keep line out of mud and sap, and wash it gently if it gets grimy. Cut out damaged sections and retie the weight when the end frays. Replace the line once the coating is worn through.

Throw line is not rated to hold people or loads. It sets the line that holds you, so inspect your climbing system and anchor, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the drop zone clear.
Keep a short length of spare line in your kit for retying weights, and inspect the knot at the weight end each morning. A worn knot that lets go mid-throw sends the weight somewhere you did not plan.

body.h: Picking DynaGlide rope or another line
p: Throw lines differ in diameter, stiffness and coating. Thinner, slicker lines go farther and add less drag; stiffer lines tangle less; softer lines are easier to grip. DynaGlide sits on the slick, smooth end of that range, which suits climbers who isolate crotches often and work the line through the canopy.

If you are new to setting lines, it helps to try a couple of lines and see which one suits your throwing style. Once you find one you like, buy a second hank as a spare. Lines get stuck in trees and cut by saws, and a spare in the truck means the job keeps moving.

faq.q: Is DynaGlide good with a launcher?
faq.a: Yes. A light slick throw line is a good match for pole launchers because it adds little drag.

faq.q: What weight should I pair with DynaGlide throw line?
faq.a: Use a weight you can throw accurately; many climbers carry a lighter and a heavier bag and switch as needed.

faq.q: Can DynaGlide be used for rigging?
faq.a: No. It is a throw line only. Use rated rigging rope for loads.

name: Petzl Jet Throw Weight
title: Petzl Jet Throw Weight for Arborists
meta: The Petzl Jet throw weight is a streamlined, durable throw bag for setting climbing lines. Pick a weight, pair it with throw line and set lines faster.

p: Lighter throw weights travel farther on a hand throw and are easier to pull back. Heavier ones punch through foliage and drop better, and they help pull line down through tight forks. Many climbers carry two throw weights, one light and one heavier, so they can switch without retying.
Pair the Jet with a slick line from our throw line section.

The Jet's streamlined shape helps it pass between twigs and leaves without hanging up, and the tough cover stands up to repeated throws and bark contact. When choosing among throw weights, also think about the throw line you use: thin slick lines pair well with lighter weights for long throws.

Keep people, vehicles and windows out of the landing zone and call out before each throw. Wear a helmet when throwing under the canopy. Inspect the cover and attachment point for wear. Throw lines and weights are used to set climbing lines, not to hold a climber. Always inspect the climbing line and anchor you install, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the drop zone clear when throwing.
Store the weight clipped to your throw line bag so it is ready to go and does not get lost in the truck.

faq.q: Which weight should I start with?
faq.a: A middle weight is a good start. Go lighter for long throws, heavier for dense foliage.

faq.q: Can I use the Jet with a launcher?
faq.a: Check Petzl's guidance and the launcher maker's recommendations before using any weight in a launcher.

name: Arborist Rope Climbing Kit
title: Tree Climbing Kit for Arborists: Rope Climbing Kits
h1: Tree Climbing Kit: Arborist Rope Climbing Kits
meta: An arborist tree climbing kit bundles saddle, rope, hitch cord, carabiners and pulley so you can start climbing on rope. What to look for and typical price.
tagline: A matched set of tree climbing gear to get you up and working on rope.
summary: A tree climbing kit puts the core tree climbing gear an arborist needs in one package: saddle, climbing rope, friction hitch cord, carabiners, pulley and lanyard. Buying a kit means the parts are chosen to work together and nothing is left out.
highlights: Saddle, climbing line and hitch cord in one package
Locking carabiners and a hitch-tending pulley
Flip line or lanyard for positioning
A solid base you can upgrade over time
specs: Saddle, climbing rope, hitch cord, carabiners, pulley, lanyard
Moving rope (DdRT); SRT parts vary by kit
Helmet, throw line kit, hand saw

body.h: What's in a tree climbing gear kit
p: A typical arborist climbing kit includes a saddle, a length of arborist climbing rope, a friction hitch cord, locking carabiners, a hitch-tending pulley, and a lanyard or flip line. Some kits add throw line and a weight, a rope bag or a helmet.

The value of a kit is fit. The rope diameter suits the hitch cord, the carabiners suit the saddle bridge, and the pulley suits the hitch. Piecing a set together yourself is fine, but it is easy to end up with parts that do not work well together.

Arborist climbing kits also save time at checkout. Instead of researching every carabiner and hitch cord separately, you start with a working set and learn what you like before upgrading pieces one at a time.

Kits suit new climbers building a first set, crews outfitting a new employee, and climbers who want a backup system for the truck. Experienced climbers often buy individual pieces, but a kit is still a quick way to set up a second climber.

Before buying, think about how you will climb. Moving rope (DdRT) setups are common for beginners and for pruning work. Stationary rope (SRT) is popular with experienced climbers for access. Check whether a kit includes the hardware for the system you plan to use.

If you are outfitting a crew, consider standardizing on one arborist tree climbing kit. When every climber uses the same system, it is easier to inspect gear, train new climbers and perform an aerial rescue, because everyone knows how the other climber's system works.

Saddle fit matters most. Measure your waist and legs and check the saddle's size range. Next look at rope: length should be at least twice the height of the trees you climb, plus some spare. Make sure every carabiner is a locking model suitable for life support.
Add a helmet, eye protection and a hand saw if they are not included. A starter throw line kit is the next thing most new climbers add.
Check what the kit leaves out as well. Common extras include a rope bag, a second lanyard, and a throw line cube. Plan your budget so the essentials are covered before you spend on upgrades.

Climbing gear is life-support equipment. Every part should meet ANSI Z133 and the applicable product standards, and you should follow each manufacturer's instructions. Inspect your system before every climb and retire anything damaged.
A kit does not replace training. Learn to climb with a qualified instructor or experienced climber, practice aerial rescue, and never climb alone.

Build your inspection routine around the kit from day one. Check the saddle stitching, rope sheath, hitch cord and carabiner gates before each climb, and keep a simple log of when each piece went into service.

faq.q: Is a tree climbing kit good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the beginner is being trained. A kit removes the guesswork of matching parts.

faq.q: How long should my climbing rope be?
faq.a: At least twice the height of the tallest tie-in you expect, plus a margin. Many climbers start with 120 to 150 feet.

faq.q: Can I use a kit for SRT?
faq.a: Some kits are set up for SRT or include parts that work for both. Check the contents before buying.

name: Arbortec Scafell Lite Chainsaw Boots, Lime Green
title: Arbortec Boots: Scafell Lite Chainsaw Boots, Lime Green
h1: Arbortec Boots: Scafell Lite Chainsaw Boots, Lime Green
meta: Arbortec boots built for saw work: the Scafell Lite chainsaw boot pairs cut protection with a lighter build and a lime finish. Fit tips and typical price.
tagline: Lighter cut-protective chainsaw boots in high-visibility lime green.
summary: The Scafell Lite is one of the best-known Arbortec boots, a chainsaw boot built to be lighter than traditional protective logging boots. The lime green finish makes you easier to spot on the ground and in the canopy.
highlights: Lighter build for long days on your feet
Lugged sole for grip on slopes and brush
Suitable for ground work and climbing
specs: Check the label for cut protection class

p: Your feet are close to the bar every time you buck a log, limb on the ground or drop a top. Chainsaw boots use cut-resistant layers in the upper that are designed to clog or slow a running chain. Ordinary leather work boots do not do that.

ANSI Z133 calls for appropriate foot protection when running a saw, and many crews now standardize on chainsaw-rated boots for anyone who touches a saw. Check the boot label for its protection class and make sure it matches your employer's requirements.
Chainsaw boots also carry protective toe caps and tough soles. That protects against dropped rounds, rolling logs and the sharp stubs left after cleanup.

body.h: What makes the Scafell Lite different
p: Traditional chainsaw boots can feel like ski boots. The design of these scafell lite chainsaw boots focuses on cutting weight and adding flexibility, so they are easier to wear for a full day of walking, dragging brush and running the chipper.
The lime green finish adds visibility. On busy roadside jobs and in thick brush, anything that helps the ground crew and the climber see each other is worth having.

Lighter boots matter more than most people think. Over a day of walking between the truck, the chipper and the drop zone, a heavy boot adds up to real fatigue. Arbortec boots like the Scafell Lite aim to keep protection without that penalty, which is why many climbers wear them both on the ground and in the tree.

Try boots on with the socks you wear on the job. You want a snug heel, room to wiggle your toes, and no pressure on the top of the foot when you kneel. Break them in on light days before a long removal.

If you climb on spurs, check that the boot sole is stiff enough for the stirrup. Many climbers keep a separate pair of climbing boots for spur work. Compare other arborist boots if you need a different style.
Lace them firmly around the ankle for support on slopes, and leave a little room across the forefoot so your feet can swell during a hot day without pinching.

Clean off mud and sap after each job, let the boots dry away from direct heat, and treat the leather as the maker recommends. Retire boots that have taken a chain cut, since the protective layers have done their job and will not protect the same way again.

Check soles for wear and separation and replace boots when the tread no longer grips. Remember that boots are only one part of saw PPE: chaps or chainsaw pants, eye and hearing protection, gloves and a helmet are all required under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Are Arbortec Scafell Lite boots chainsaw protective?
faq.a: Yes, they are made as chainsaw boots. Check the label for the exact protection class before relying on them for a specific requirement.

faq.q: Can I climb in Scafell Lite boots?
faq.a: Many climbers wear them on rope. For spur work, make sure the sole is stiff enough to support the stirrup.

faq.q: Do Arbortec boots run true to size?
faq.a: Fit varies by foot. Try them on with your work socks and check heel hold and toe room.

meta: The Arbpro Cervino Wood S3 steel toe chainsaw boot from Andrew is a sturdy leather saw boot for forestry and tree work. Fit, care tips and typical US price.
tagline: Rugged leather chainsaw boots from Andrew for forestry and tree crews.
summary: The Arbpro Cervino Wood S3 steel toe chainsaw boot is made by the Italian bootmaker Andrew and sold through Arbpro. It is a sturdy leather chainsaw boot built for steep ground, brush and full days running a saw.
highlights: Aggressive lugged sole for slopes and brush
Made by Andrew, sold through Arbpro
specs: Check the label for cut protection class

body.h: A forestry boot for tree work
p: Andrew boots come out of the Italian mountain-boot tradition, and the Cervino shows it. It is a high, supportive leather boot with a deep lugged sole that bites into slopes, wet leaves and loose ground. That suits tree crews who spend the day climbing banks, dragging brush and standing on logs.

The Cervino is a chainsaw boot, so cut-protective layers sit in the upper where a running chain is most likely to contact the foot. Check the label for its protection class to confirm it meets your employer's rules.
The deep sole also helps on the stump and on logs, where a smooth sole slides. When you are standing on a log to buck it, secure footing is a big part of keeping your feet away from the chain.

The steel toe protects against rolling logs, dropped rounds and the occasional misplaced log tong. High ankle support helps on uneven ground and when you carry heavy gear. The trade-off is weight: this is a substantial boot, closer to a mountaineering boot than a sneaker.
If you want something lighter for mostly flat suburban work, compare the Arbortec Scafell Lite.
The extra weight pays off on rough ground and long days on your feet, where the support reduces ankle strain. On flat lawns and suburban jobs, some crews find a lighter boot more comfortable.

Try the Andrew Cervino with your work socks. Leather boots like this need a break-in period, so wear them on easier days before a long job. Lace firmly around the ankle and leave a little more room over the forefoot.
If you climb on spurs, check that the sole is stiff enough for your stirrups.
Andrew boots come in European sizing, so check the size chart carefully and try them on if you can. If you are between sizes, consider your sock thickness and whether you will wear an insole.
Wear them around the yard or on short jobs for the first week. Stiff leather softens with use, and breaking them in slowly prevents blisters on your first long removal day.

Clean mud and sap off after work, dry the boots slowly away from direct heat, and treat the leather regularly. Replace boots that have taken a chainsaw cut or show worn-through soles. Foot protection is part of your saw PPE alongside chaps, eye and ear protection, gloves and a helmet, as described in ANSI Z133.
Like any chainsaw boot, the Cervino is a backup, not a license to get careless. Keep your feet out of the cut path, plant both feet before cutting, and keep the bar away from your body.

faq.q: Who makes the Arbpro Cervino boot?
faq.a: It is made by Andrew, an Italian bootmaker, and sold through Arbpro.

faq.q: Is the Cervino a steel toe boot?
faq.a: Yes, the Cervino Wood is a steel toe chainsaw boot. Check the label for its full protection rating.

faq.q: Are Andrew boots heavy?
faq.a: They are sturdy leather boots, so they weigh more than lighter synthetic saw boots. Many users accept that for the support and grip.

title: Arbpro Boots: Clip N Step Work Boots
meta: Arbpro boots for tree work: the Clip N Step boot is built for arborists who climb, rig and work the ground all day. Fit notes, care advice and typical US price.

summary: The Clip N Step is one of the Arbpro boots built for tree work, aimed at climbers and ground workers who need a sturdy, supportive boot. It suits crews who move between the rope, the stump and the chipper all day.
highlights: Grippy sole for slopes and brush

p: Arborists ask a lot of a boot: grip on bark and wet ground, support when standing on a limb, and comfort through a ten-hour day. Arbpro designs its boots around that mix. The Clip N Step is aimed at climbers who also spend real time on the ground.

Check the product label for toe protection and whether the boot carries chainsaw cut protection. If you run a saw on the ground, ANSI Z133 calls for suitable foot protection. See all arborist boots to compare.

Good arborist boots pay you back in fewer sore feet and fewer slips. Look for firm heel hold, a sole with deep lugs that clears mud, and an upper stiff enough to protect your foot when you stand on a limb or a rope wraps around your ankle. Arbpro boots are built with those details in mind.

Try boots with your work socks and check heel hold and toe room. Break them in before a long job. Clean off mud and sap, dry slowly away from heat, and treat leather as the maker recommends. Replace boots with worn soles or damaged uppers.
Inspect boots regularly and keep a spare pair in the truck for wet days. Dry feet stay warmer and blister less.

faq.q: Are Clip N Step boots chainsaw protective?

name: Arborwear Neck Warmer
title: Arborwear Neckwarmer for Cold Tree Work
meta: The Arborwear neckwarmer keeps cold air off your neck and face on winter climbs and ground work, and fits under a helmet and jacket collar. See typical price.
tagline: A simple fleece neck tube that keeps the wind off on winter jobs.
summary: The Arborwear neckwarmer is a simple tube of warm fabric that keeps wind and cold off your neck and lower face. It slips on under a helmet and jacket collar without the loose ends of a scarf.
highlights: Tube design with no loose ends
Pull up over your face in wind
Packs into a pocket when you warm up

body.h: Why a neck warmer beats a scarf
p: Winter tree work means long stretches standing still on the ground and sudden bursts of hard work in the canopy. A scarf is a hazard around saws, chippers and moving rope, since loose ends can catch. A neckwarmer is a closed tube with nothing hanging, so it stays put.
Pull it down when you are working hard and up over your chin and nose when you are stopped in the wind. It takes up almost no room in a pocket.

Arborwear makes gear for people who work outside in trees, and the neckwarmer is one of the simplest pieces in the lineup. It is a practical answer to cold mornings at the chipper, wind on an exposed climb, and drizzle running down your collar.
It also cuts the wind when you ride in an open truck bed or drive the loader on a cold morning, and it covers the gap at the back of your neck where cold air sneaks in under a hood.

Cold-weather tree work is all about layers you can adjust without stripping down. Start with a moisture-wicking base, add an insulating mid layer like a heavy hoodie, and finish with a wind-resistant shell. The neck warmer seals the gap at the collar, which is where a lot of heat escapes.
Pair it with a warm stocking cap on the ground, or wear it under a helmet liner when climbing.

A neck warmer also helps when you are switching between climbing and ground work. When you descend sweaty and stand around in the cold, pulling the tube up keeps the chill off while your body cools down slowly.
On the coldest days, add a thin balaclava or helmet liner that your helmet maker approves, and use the neckwarmer to cover the gap between the liner and your jacket.

It fits under a climbing helmet chin strap without bunching, but make sure the strap still sits snug and the helmet stays level. Keep the fabric clear of your face when wearing eye protection, since breath can fog lenses.
Like any clothing around a chipper, keep it tucked in and close-fitting. Never reach into a chipper infeed, and follow ANSI Z133 and the chipper manufacturer's instructions.
If you climb with hearing protection or a radio headset, check that the neckwarmer does not get in the way of the earmuff seal or the microphone.
Machine wash and air dry. Skip fabric softener, which can reduce the fabric's ability to move moisture. Have a spare in the truck for wet days.
Keep two or three in rotation over winter so you always have a dry one. They take up almost no room in a gear bag or glove box.

faq.q: Can I wear a neckwarmer under a climbing helmet?
faq.a: Yes. It sits low on the neck and works under most chin straps. Make sure the helmet still fits correctly.

faq.q: Is a neckwarmer safe around a chipper?

name: Arborwear Stocking Cap
title: Arborwear Stocking Hat for Winter Tree Work
meta: The Arborwear stocking hat is a warm, close-fitting knit cap for cold mornings on the ground, at the chipper or under a hood. What to know and typical price.
tagline: A warm, close-fitting knit cap for cold mornings on tree jobs.
summary: The Arborwear stocking hat is a warm knit cap made for cold mornings loading the truck, running the chipper and working the ground. It fits close to the head so it stays put and works under a hood.
highlights: Easy to stash in a jacket pocket

p: Every tree crew has a pile of stocking caps in the truck by November. A good stocking cap keeps your head warm through the coldest part of the morning, when you are loading gear, setting up cones and waiting for the climber to tie in. This one fits close, so it does not ride up when you bend over to drag brush.

Stocking caps have a lot of names: beanie, toque, knit hat. If you have been searching for a stockingcap near me, the one that matters is the one that stays on your head and keeps you warm when you are standing around.

Arborwear designs its gear for tree workers, and the stocking cap reflects that: simple, warm and tough enough to take getting stuffed in a pocket all day. It comes off a tree crew's dashboard more often than any other piece of winter gear.

A good stocking cap should be thick enough to block wind but not so bulky it will not fit in a pocket. It should also hold its shape after months of washing and being stuffed in a coat. This one covers the ears fully, which is where cold mornings hurt most.

A knit cap is ground gear. Do not wear a thick stocking cap under a climbing helmet or hard hat unless the helmet maker allows it, since it can change how the helmet fits and protects. For climbing, look for a thin helmet liner designed for your helmet.
On the ground, pull it on during breaks and stash it in a pocket when you start working hard. Pair it with a neck warmer for windy days.
Many climbers take the stocking hat off right before they gear up and leave it clipped to their bag or in the truck. When they come down, it goes right back on to hold heat while they cool off.
You lose heat fast from your head and neck when you are wet and not moving. Combine a stocking cap, neck warmer, heavy hoodie and shell, and you can adjust warmth quickly without changing clothes.
Keep loose clothing away from chippers and running saws. ANSI Z133 and the chipper manufacturer's instructions apply to everything you wear near the infeed.
On wet days, a knit cap under your jacket hood keeps the hood from sitting directly on your head, and you stay warmer when the outer layer gets soaked.
Wash cold and lay flat to dry to keep the knit in shape. Keep a spare in the truck in case one gets soaked.
If the knit starts to pill or stretch out after a few seasons, it still makes a good spare for the glove box.

faq.q: Can I wear a stocking cap under my helmet?
faq.a: Only if your helmet maker allows it. A thick cap can change helmet fit, so use a thin approved liner for climbing.

faq.q: Does it fit large heads?
faq.a: Knit caps stretch, so one size fits most adults.

faq.q: Is a stocking hat the same as a beanie?
faq.a: Yes, the terms are often used for the same close-fitting knit cap.

body.h: A Husqvarna trucker hat for everyday wear
p: Husqvarna hats are a fixture in saw shops and on tree crews. The Utforskare is a trucker cap with a structured front panel and a mesh back, so it holds its shape and breathes when you are working hard in the sun.
Utforskare means explorer in Swedish, a nod to the brand's roots. The cap is a simple way to show which saws you run.
Husqvarna hats come in a range of styles, from beanies to trucker caps. The trucker style is the summer favorite because the mesh back lets heat escape when you are working hard in the sun.
The front panel carries the Husqvarna logo, so it pairs with any other Husqvarna gear you wear on the job. The curved brim keeps sun off your face and out of your eyes when you look up at the canopy.

body.h: Where it fits on the job
p: A cap is ground gear. It keeps the sun out of your eyes when you are watching the climber, sharpening chains, running the chipper or driving between jobs. It is not head protection. When a climber is working overhead, the whole ground crew should be in helmets, as ANSI Z133 requires.
Many people keep a cap on until the helmet goes on, then clip it to their bag. Browse more hats and caps for cold-weather options.
On hot days, a breathable cap and plenty of water go a long way. Shade your eyes while running the chipper or watching the climber, and swap to your helmet as soon as anyone goes up.
The adjustable back fits most heads. Hand wash the cap with mild soap, rinse and let it air dry on a form so the front panel keeps its shape. Avoid the dryer and the dishwasher.
Sweat and sawdust will wear any cap down. A couple of spares in the truck mean you always have a dry one.
If your cap gets soaked in sweat daily, rinse it in clean water at the end of the week. That keeps salt and sawdust from building up in the sweatband and stiffening the fabric.

Look for a cap that fits snug enough not to blow off in wind or when you bend over, with an adjustable back so you can loosen it on hot days. A structured front holds its shape after being stuffed in a bag, and a curved brim keeps sun off your face.

A Husqvarna trucker hat makes an easy gift for anyone on a tree crew or anyone who runs a Husqvarna saw at home. It is also a simple way to keep a few spare caps in the truck for crew members who forget theirs.

faq.q: Is the Husqvarna Utforskare hat adjustable?

faq.q: Can I wear a cap under a helmet?

faq.q: How should I wash a trucker hat?
faq.a: Hand wash with mild soap and air dry on a form.

A double thick sweatshirt is built for the work: two layers of fabric that trap more heat and take more abuse before they wear through at the elbows and cuffs. On a cold morning dragging brush, that extra layer is the difference between comfortable and miserable.
Arborwear built its name on tree-work clothing, and the Double Thick hooded sweatshirt is one of its best-known pieces. Many crews treat it as their go-to winter layer.

The extra fabric also helps with abrasion. Hoodies on tree crews get dragged across bark, rubbed by rope and snagged on brush, and a single-layer sweatshirt can wear through at the forearms in one season. The double thick hoodie lasts longer under that kind of use.
This listing is the black arbor hoodie in large. Black hides sawdust, bar oil and chipper grime better than lighter colors. If you prefer navy, see the navy Double Thick hoodie.

Around chippers, loose clothing is a serious hazard. Keep sleeves snug, never reach into the infeed, and follow ANSI Z133 and the chipper manufacturer's instructions. A hoodie is not high-visibility clothing; add a vest for roadside work.
On wet days, wear the hoodie under a waterproof shell. Heavy fleece holds water when soaked, so keeping it dry keeps it warm.
Remember that a hoodie is not a substitute for PPE. When you run a saw, wear chaps or chainsaw pants, eye and hearing protection, gloves and a helmet, as ANSI Z133 requires.
Wash cold, inside out, and tumble dry low or hang dry to limit shrinkage. Skip fabric softener. With reasonable care, a double sweatshirt like this should last through several winters of hard use.
If the cuffs or elbows wear out after years of use, the hoodie can still serve as a shop or yard layer. Many tree workers keep an older one in the truck as a spare.

faq.q: How warm is a double thick hoodie?

faq.q: Does the Double Thick hoodie shrink?
faq.a: Like most cotton-blend fleece it can shrink slightly. Wash cold and dry low or hang dry.

faq.q: Is it safe to climb in a hoodie?
faq.a: Yes, if the hood and drawstrings are managed and your helmet still fits correctly.

faq.q: Will it shrink?

Compare other tree climbing pants if you need a heavier or lighter fabric.

Heavy duty elastic handles the extra weight of protective pants without stretching out after a few weeks.

Adjust so the pants sit at your natural waist without pulling your shoulders. Check clips and elastic regularly and replace them when they stretch out or the clips weaken. Chainsaw pants are part of saw PPE under ANSI Z133; keep them in good condition and retire any pair that has taken a cut.
Keep the suspenders clean and away from bar oil and fuel, which break down elastic. Inspect clips before each job so a strap does not let go when you are in the middle of a cut.

name: Silky Sugoi Replacement Blade
title: Silky Sugoi Replacement Blade: Fresh Teeth for Your Saw
meta: A Silky Sugoi replacement blade brings your Sugoi back to full cutting speed. Match the blade length to your saw and swap it in minutes. Typical price.
tagline: A factory replacement blade to bring a dull Sugoi back to full speed.
summary: A Silky Sugoi replacement blade is the fastest way to get a dull or damaged Sugoi cutting like new again. Silky replacement saw blades swap onto the existing handle, so you keep your scabbard and grip and only pay for fresh teeth.

Match the length to your saw
specs: Available to match Sugoi 330, 360 and 420 mm saws

p: Silky teeth are impulse hardened, which keeps them sharp for a long time but means they are not meant to be filed like a Western saw. When the blade starts to wander, burn, or need real effort on wood it used to slice through, it is time for a new one. A blade with a kink, bent tip or broken teeth should be replaced right away.
Replacing the blade costs much less than a new saw. You keep the handle, which is often in good shape long after the teeth are done, and the scabbard you already have fits the same size blade.

Climbers who cut daily often go through blades several times a year. Dirty wood, sandy bark near the ground, and hitting nails or wire all dull teeth quickly. Having a spare blade in the truck means you can swap it in at lunch instead of struggling through the afternoon.

The Sugoi comes in more than one blade length, so check your saw before ordering. The length is printed on the blade and handle. A replacement saw blade in the wrong length will not fit your scabbard properly and may not seat in the handle.
Shopping for a different saw instead? See the full Silky Sugoi hand saw or browse other replacement blades.
If you are not sure which saw you have, look for the model name and length printed on the blade near the handle. When in doubt, compare the old blade with the new one before throwing it away.

Remove the screw or bolt holding the blade in the handle, slide the old blade out, and fit the new one so it seats fully. Tighten the fastener firmly and check for play before cutting. Wear gloves while handling the blade, since new teeth are very sharp.
Dispose of the old blade safely by wrapping the teeth in tape or cardboard.
After installing the new blade, make a few test cuts on the ground before taking the saw aloft. That confirms the blade is seated and the fastener is tight.

Clean pitch off the blade after work with a resin cleaner and wipe on a light coat of oil to prevent rust. Do not twist the saw in a cut or use it to pry. Hand saws are sharp enough to cause serious cuts. Keep the blade in its scabbard when not cutting, wear gloves, and cut away from your body and your climbing line. Follow ANSI Z133 and get trained before cutting aloft.
Store the saw dry and in its scabbard. A rusty blade drags in the cut, and moisture trapped in the scabbard can spot the steel overnight.

faq.q: Can I sharpen a Silky Sugoi blade?
faq.a: Silky teeth are impulse hardened and are generally replaced rather than sharpened. Check Silky's guidance before attempting it.

faq.q: Will any Silky blade fit my Sugoi?
faq.a: No. Use a Sugoi blade in the same length as your saw.

faq.q: How long does a Sugoi blade last?
faq.a: It depends on species, dirt and technique. Many climbers replace blades several times over the life of a handle.

Silky's reputation comes from Japanese steel and precise tooth geometry, and the GomTaro brings that to a saw at a more accessible price. For crews equipping several workers, that makes it easy to put a good saw in everyone's hands.

The 300 mm blade handles small to medium limbs well. Use it for crown cleaning, raising and reducing on rope, pruning young trees, and landscape work. On the ground it is handy for limbing brush before it goes to the chipper.
Let the teeth do the work. Pushing hard or twisting in the kerf can bend the blade. Make a small undercut first on larger limbs to prevent bark tearing.
On the ground, the straight blade is also handy for cutting roots, small stumps and brush near the soil line, though dirt and grit dull teeth quickly. Keep a second saw for dirty cuts if you can.
The saw is light enough to carry all day on a belt. Ground workers who do a lot of cleanup pruning on shrubs and small trees often keep one clipped on at all times.
The GomTaro comes with a scabbard that clips to a belt or saddle. Always return the saw to the scabbard before moving in the tree. Check the scabbard retention regularly so the saw cannot fall out.
Compare it with curved saws like the Silky Sugoi in our hand saws and scabbards section.
Scabbards wear too. If the retention clip loosens or the scabbard cracks, replace it so you do not lose the saw from height.

Clean sap off the blade with resin cleaner and wipe with light oil. When the teeth are dull, replace the blade rather than filing it. Hand saws are sharp enough to cause serious cuts. Keep the blade in its scabbard when not cutting, wear gloves, and cut away from your body and your climbing line. Follow ANSI Z133 and get trained before cutting aloft.
Store the saw dry and in its scabbard. Moisture left on the blade leads to rust spots that slow the cut.

faq.q: Is a straight saw good for climbing?

body.h: Why the Sugoi is a climber's favorite
p: Sugoi means amazing in Japanese, and the name fits the way it cuts. The blade is curved, so it pulls itself into the wood on each stroke, and it is taper ground, thinner at the back than at the teeth. That taper reduces binding in the kerf, so the saw keeps moving on green wood and big limbs.

The teeth are large and impulse hardened, which keeps them sharp for a long time. The result is a Silky arborist saw that handles limbs many climbers would otherwise reach for a top-handle saw to cut.
The handle is rubberized and shaped to fill the hand, which helps control on long cuts and keeps the saw from twisting when you hit a knot.

That cutting speed is why the Silky Sugoi hand saw shows up on the saddles of so many climbers. When you can finish a cut quickly with a hand saw, you avoid starting a chainsaw in an awkward position and reduce the time you spend reaching out on a limb.

The Sugoi Pro 330 is the most popular length for climbing. It is long enough for real limbs and short enough to manage on a saddle. The 360 and 420 mm versions add reach and capacity for removal work and big pruning cuts, at the cost of a longer scabbard.
If your saw is getting dull, a Sugoi replacement blade brings it back without replacing the handle.
Silky also uses tooth patterns suited to green wood, which is what climbers cut most. On dry, dead wood, the saw still cuts fast but the teeth wear quicker.

Let the saw do the work. Use long, smooth pull strokes and light pressure. On bigger limbs, make an undercut first to stop bark tearing, then finish from the top. Avoid twisting the blade in the kerf, which can kink it.
Keep your free hand and climbing line out of the cutting path, and plan where the piece will fall before you cut.
On larger limbs, use your free hand to steady yourself, not to hold the limb near the cut. Let the piece fall clear rather than trying to catch it.
The Sugoi comes with a scabbard that clips to a belt or saddle. Put the saw away every time you move in the tree. Clean resin off the blade after work and wipe on a little oil to prevent rust.

Hand saws are sharp enough to cause serious cuts. Keep the blade in its scabbard when not cutting, wear gloves, and cut away from your body and your climbing line. Follow ANSI Z133 and get trained before cutting aloft.
Replace the scabbard if the retention weakens, and keep the saw on the side of your saddle that suits your cutting hand.

faq.q: What size Silky Sugoi should I buy?
faq.a: The 330 mm is the most popular for climbing. Go longer for removals and larger limbs.

faq.q: Can a Sugoi blade be sharpened?
faq.a: Sugoi teeth are impulse hardened and are normally replaced rather than sharpened.

faq.q: Is the Sugoi worth the price?
faq.a: For daily climbers and pro pruners, its speed and durability make it one of the most popular hand saws on tree crews.
